14: PETER. No, I feel I shall die to-day, I feel it. [ Leans back and shuts his eyes ].
13: MATRYÓNA. If God don't take a soul, the soul can't go out. Death and life are in God's will, Peter Ignátitch. You can't be sure of death either. Maybe you'll recover yet. There was a man in our village just like that, at the very point of death …
12: PETER. Let me sit here a bit for the last time. The air's so stuffy inside. Oh, how bad I feel! Oh, my heart's burning.… Oh, if death would only come.
11: ANÍSYA [ from inside ] She went then and there. Come inside, won't you? I'll help you in.
10: MATRYÓNA [ aside ] There now, he's remembered!
9: PETER [ to Anísya inside the house ] Has Nan gone?
8: MATRYÓNA. Why, if it's money, or something, you can leave orders.
7: PETER. There'll be no one to manage things! She's not steady. Has her head full of folly—why, I know all about it, I know. And my girl is silly and young. I've got the homestead together, and there's no one to attend to things. One can't help feeling it. [ Whimpers ].
6: MATRYÓNA. Oh well, Peter Ignátitch, it's God's will you know, you've had communion, and you'll have unction, God willing. Your missus is a wise woman, the Lord be thanked; she'll give you a good burial, and have prayers said for your soul, all most respectable! And my son, he'll look after things meanwhile.
5: PETER. My last hour has come.
4: MATRYÓNA. Ah yes, Peter Ignátitch, now I look at you I see, as the saying has it, “Sickness lives where men live.” You've shrivelled, shrivelled, all to nothing, poor dear, now I come to look at you. Seems illness does not add to good looks.
2: PETER. How do you do? MATRYÓNA [ bowing ] How d'you do, my benefactor; how d'you do, my precious … still ill, I see. And my old man, he's that sorry! “Go,” says he, “see how he's getting on.” He sends his respects to you. [ Bows again ].
0: PETER. Well then, light it. [ Anísya goes into the house. Matryóna comes up to the porch ].
